analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 430, Samuel M. Atkinson et al. Petitioners v. Sinclair Refining Company. Number 434, Sinclair Refining Company v. Samuel M. Atkinson et al. Mr. Cornfield. Please, court, this case comes before this court on the original pleadings filed by the employer in the district court for the Northern District of Indiana. In that light, we must take the pleadings as well pleaded at this juncture in the litigation. The original complaint filed by the employer was in three counts. First was a suit by the employer against an international union and its local affiliate for breach of a no-strike clause of their bargaining agreement requesting damages. The second count was against 12 local union committeemen for instigating and participating in the alleged breach of the no-strike clause. I might say that the allegations of fact against the international and local union in count one were the same as the allegations against the 12 local union committeemen in count two. Count three of the complaint was against all the defendants, against the international, the local affiliates, and the 12 local union committeemen. And it was a request for a blanket injunction operating into the future. At this point, I wish to comment that the time this suit was brought, there was no alleged breach of the no-strike clause then occurring. I wish to state the request for the injunction contained in count three. It's against the organizations and the individual defendants, each of them, their agents, servants, counselors, and all to whom notice hereof may come, being joined and restrained from aiding, abetting, fomenting, advising, participating in, ratifying, or condoning any strike, stoppage of work, slowdown, or any other disruption of, or interference with normal employment, or normal operation or production, by any employee within the bargaining unit at the employer's East Chicago, Indiana refinery. I might add that the broad scope of the requested injunction presumably would include new employees which may be hired at the plant in the indefinite future. I presume that the employer would hand each new employee a copy of the injunction order along with his employment application. We filed a motion to dismiss these three counts. The district court, after reconsideration, dismissed count two, that is the action against the individual defendants in their individual capacities and the requested injunction, leaving count one. We'll recess now, mister. Before the recess, I had indicated that the district court had dismissed count two of the complaint as the action against the individual local officials and count three of the complaint requests for the injunction. The case at that point went before the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's decision as regards count three and the injunction request and overruled the district court in its decision to dismiss count two. I might say that the Seventh Circuit's opinion as to the action against the individuals indicates that it is the Seventh Circuit's view that the individuals might be held responsible for breach of the no-strike clause if the union were not. Now, in looking over the employer's complaint, Sinclair's claim for relief sounds deceptively simple and, I believe, to many ears eminently fair. But we submit that if individuals, local union officials, are to be brought into state courts or into federal courts under diversity of citizenship jurisdiction. And if the injunction requested here to operate into the indefinite future is granted, a Pandora's box of confusing litigation will ensue before federal and state courts. We have argued rather extensively, we believe in our briefs, that the net result of the suit against the individuals and the request for an injunction is continuing conflict with the National Labor Relations Board and the jurisdiction of the federal courts to enforce and develop substantive law under their powers granted by Congress under Section 301 of the Taft-Hartley Act. Furthermore, the requested injunction not only guarantees the recurrence of such conflicts into the unforeseeable future, but flies in the face of the clear language and the spirit of long-standing... Yes, Mr. Justice Brennan. That's right. I believe that the employer acknowledges that individuals cannot be sued under Section 301 under the clear language of that section which allows suits only against labor organizations and only against the organizational assets. Going back to the injunction request, if... Your request for a stay? No, I'm talking about the employer's requested injunction into the future. Against all the defendants, labor organizations, individuals, their agents, counselors, servants, et cetera. I might say this, that the employer's requested relief is if allowed would interject trial judges, all over the country into labor controversies, forcing them to impose their varying views on social policy in an area which properly must lie within the discretion of Congress. Now, I would like in this oral presentation to discuss the implications of the requested relief by the employer. First, I would like to discuss count two of the complaint. That is, the request for damages against the individual local union officials under a tort, common law tort theory, based on joint and several liability. First, the employer contends that we entered into a collective bargaining contract between the unions, that is, the international and its local affiliate, that this contract contains a no-strike pledge. The employer maintains that we submitted to an arbitration procedure and in return we extracted from the unions a no-strike obligation. Now, I might say that the employer does not mention also that the unions in turn extracted a no-lockout obligation on the part of the employers. If there is a quid pro quo for anything here, it is the no-strike and the quid pro quo for the no-strike is the no-lockout obligation on the part of the employer. Is the arbitration provisions, are they comparable to those in Lincoln Mills? The arbitration provisions set out a grievance procedure. They first define the grievances as covering all wages, hours, and working conditions and then establish a grievance procedure and then provide for arbitration. There is this added clause in this contract which is not discussed in the employer's brief. Article 27 of the contract also provides for so-called general disputes directly between the highest level of the employer hierarchy and the highest level of the international arbitration. I don't want to disturb the train of your argument but it would help me if I knew precisely what issues were before the arbitrator at the time this suit in the district court was filed by the employer. The employer after the work stoppage occurred docked the local union committeemen for the time of the work stoppage claiming that they were not fulfilling their responsibilities as local union officials. The employer also took certain action against the local union officials in the form of saying that from now on you will not have free reigns to operate around the plant and process grievances. At the time the suit was filed these grievances had been submitted to arbitration or at least they had gone through all the stages of the grievance procedure and there had been an understanding to submit these to arbitration. A joint agreement? A joint agreement an arbitrator has not been selected as yet. There is this confusion I believe by my saying the employer's brief. There are two arbitration issues here. One is that we request a stay based on the fact that the activities if any of the local union officials has been brought to arbitration by virtue of the grievances we file. But we also say further as in Drake Bakeries that the employer should initiate arbitration against the unions as to the question of the breach of the no strike clause. I guess that's the thing. That's right. I would like if possible to reserve the question of arbitration to the last since it's been argued rather extensively in Drake Bakeries and we feel two rather important issues in addition here. Going on from the contract, the employer says I negotiated a no strike clause with the international local affiliate. Now the employer argues that during this contract term a work stoppage occurs and is participated in by over half the plan. The employer alleges in his complaint that 999 employees out of the 1,700 employees at the refinery participated in this work stoppage. Now taking the complaint is well pleaded. There's no dispute about that. And the employer claims that clearly a work stoppage occurs and we are entitled to fair relief for our loss of production. And the employer reasons very simply that clearly the court's role is to assure just compensation for this loss of production. Now the employer goes on. The unions with whom we bargain, that is the international local affiliate, clearly should be held responsible for this loss of production. So they file count one of the action. a suit under section 301 of the Taft-Hartley Act against the unions. But the employer goes on further than that. And it hedges against future possibilities. The employer says, but what if we can't prove liability against the unions? A work stoppage occurred. Clearly we must be able to collect from somebody. Now here's an international organization, its local affiliate, we filed a suit against them. Whether we argue the case in the court or we argue it before an arbitrator, a la the arguments in Drake Bakeries, what if we don't win? What if we can't prove that the international or and or the local weren't responsible? A work stoppage occurs. We must be able to collect from somebody. This leads the employer to a seemingly logical conclusion that the employees themselves should be held personally responsible for the stoppage. Now the employer did not choose to sue the 999 employees because this would apparently seem absurd on its face. The employer chooses to say, well, we're only going to sue the employees who led this work stoppage. Now I might say these are the same employees who are alleged to be agents of the international and local union in count one of the complaint. Now the employer reasons we can't bring this kind of suit under section 301 because clearly the employees themselves, the local union officials aren't labor organizations. So what are we going to do? Well, it has to come in the state court some way. There must be a common law cause of action. This leads the employer to mirror his feelings of anxiety with the old English common law tort established in Lumley v. Guy. These individual union officials stand to the membership as third parties who conspired to interfere with the contractual relationship of these 999 employees, authorities, and therefore they are guilty of a common law tort. It comes into the federal court solely by virtue of diversity of citizenship. Sinclair is a foreign corporation in terms of Indiana, and all the individual members are either citizens of Indiana, some are citizens of Illinois. Illinois. Now, the employer bases his argument on the fact that if a stoppage occurs, there must be some type of legal theory which allows us to collect. And the employer then makes out a seemingly simple case for relief. We submit that this simple case of relief opens up direct issues which are in conflict with the principles of federal preemption established in Garmin and reinforced very recently by this court relative to collective bargaining agreements in Dowd Box and in Lucas Flower. Lucas Flower and Dowd Box, taken together, along with Lincoln Mills, established the principle. It is true that state courts have jurisdiction over suits for breaches of collective bargaining agreements, but the law that is to be applied must be substantive federal law developed under Section 301 as first set forth in the Lincoln Mills decision. Now, we submit whatever chain of reasoning the employer chooses to follow in establishing some basis of liability against these individuals, ultimately you're brought back to the collective bargaining agreement. And being brought back to the collective bargaining agreement, there exists only one cause of action, and that is against the labor organizations themselves under Section 301. Under the Lucas Flower decision, a state court cannot entertain an action for breach of collective bargaining contracts that is in conflict with the jurisdiction of the federal courts under Section 301. law. Now, I would like to demonstrate that whatever logical position the employer assumes you are brought back to the collective bargaining agreement, the employer alleges that the individuals, the individual local union officials, conspired, instigated, participated in breaches of the collective bargaining contract. This was the original complaint. The employer felt, we believe, that this was so blatantly under the jurisdiction of Section 301 that the employer changed his theory and said, no, it's not that they conspired to breach the collective bargaining agreement, but the collective bargaining agreement establishes 999 personal contracts containing no strike pledge by every individual running to the employer. And it is this, these contracts, that these individuals conspired to breach or instigated people to breach. Now, if the unions, under count one, whether it's in a district court or before an arbitrator, are held not to have breached the no strike clause, how can any court find that the individuals have breached the no strike clause without running into clear conflict with federal substantive law? Either the no strike clause has been breached or it hasn't been breached. And if it has been breached, it's a collective bargaining issue and it's a suit under the collective bargaining contract that must come within the purview of Section 301. But the employer may still assert that there's some basic equity involved, that a work stoppage occurs and we want to be assured compensation. The employer argues that we know we can penalize the individuals that caused or participated in the breach. We know we can threaten them with discharge. We know we can suspend them or discipline them. But that's not enough. We want to get money and under a joint and several obligation theory. Now, the employer says, you see, if we go into count one and only on count one, the unions may argue that they aren't guarantors against every work stoppage, that we would have to show that they actually, the international and or the local instigated the work stoppage, the wildcat. Now, if we can't show that, the work stoppage still occurs. I might say this. If the union is not a guarantor, it's a matter of contract interpretation whether they are guarantors. And if the union is not a guarantor and the unions are held not to have been responsible for the work stoppage, that means that there's been no violation of the no strike clause. It's clear, it seems to us. If the unions are guarantors, then the allegations account to are moved. There's no need for them. If the work stoppage occurs, there's been a breach of contract, the unions are responsible. If the unions are responsible only if they instigated the walkout, the wildcat, this is a matter of contract interpretation. Now, let us say that the court would still maintain, under some theory, it's not Lumley versus Guy, some equitable concept that the employer is still entitled to relief. We can't conceive how, but let us say this occurs. What are the consequences of this type of decision? Are individual union officials then to be forced to defend actions in state courts? The employer indicates that he should be allowed to bring suits against individuals, whether or not he has the right to bring suits against the unions. So let us say he didn't bring this suit against the unions. He just went into the Indiana state courts, under this tort theory, and sued the individuals. Does this mean then the individuals have to defend on the basis, no, I wasn't acting alone, I was acting as an agent of the union? You would then be forced to the position that individual local union officials could only defend themselves adequately in a state court by forcing their unions to be the true party's defendant. Would this mean then that the unions would have to take disciplinary action or expel these men? Because they unduly charge their unions with the violation? It's like a corporate official being sued personally and saying, no, you don't want me, I was only acting as agent for my corporation. This would be the type of defense you're forcing these type of local union officials to submit to if they have to defend tort actions in state courts or under diversity of citizenship jurisdiction in federal courts. even if a local union official would take the position in a state court that it was the union's responsibility, the state court would have to interpret, was it the union's responsibility, and again, we're brought back to the collective bargaining contract. What is the no-strike clause? What did the unions agree to? It's inescapable, it seems to us, that the issue is a collective bargaining dispute. And under Lucas and Dowd-Box, there is nothing left, if there ever was, any tort theory to be left for the state courts. As a final answer to the question of individual liability, if the employer truly believes its remedies are inadequate, it is not for the courts to mold a new bargaining agreement to meet Sinclair Refining Company's needs. The employer must return to the bargaining table if the employer feels that the no-strike commitment was inadequate. Either the employer believes the no-strike commitment is adequate, or the employer does not. Only the employer's willingness to bargain and the union's willingness to negotiate will resolve this issue. Could the union go into court to get an injunction against the employer from a lockout and directing the employer to arbitrate? I would say this, that under our arguments relating to Norris-LaGuardia Act, that so long as the Norris-LaGuardia Act is still vital, it covers all areas of labor disputes. And it is my understanding that if it were a situation that we came into court requesting an injunction against a lockout, there'd be a serious problem under Norris-LaGuardia Act. The same way it's a serious problem, as far as the employer is concerned, in attempting to get an injunction against the union. Then what is the total purport, then, of Lincoln Mills? And it substitutes arbitration for the other, the old system, only if the parties voluntarily want it? Well, I think this, Your Honor, that Lincoln Mills demonstrates that the parties have available to them a multitude of remedies which they can agree to. Now, in the situation you suppose, let us say that we sued an employer for breach of the no lockout clause. Then the employer asks for a stay because the issue should be arbitrated. I would say in that case that the employer would be entitled to arbitration if the contract is broad enough to allow for that. I'm assuming it brought more of the sunday. Yes. On the other hand, if the employer is locking out the employees and we rush into court for an injunction against that, there might be a problem because of the Norris-LaGuardia Act. Now, the court could order that the issue be arbitrated, but there would be a serious question whether the court could order the employer to open up his doors again because of the Norris-LaGuardia Act prohibitions against injunctions and legal issues. He thinks that the injunction of the court would be restricted to directing the employer to arbitration. At this point, yes. If the lockout is to be considered the same as a strike, and of course I'm not arguing that issue at this point, I'm presuming that this is implied in your questioning. Going on to the injunction question, the employer argues that aside from the assurance of money damages, the employer wants the courts to assure him that work stoppages, wildcats, will not occur in the future, so long as there's a no-strike pledge. Now, we have pointed out that this court is not a proper form, or any federal court, for the debate of social policy as to whether Norris-LaGuardia is good, that the Clayton Act was good, whether it should be amended. We have argued extensively, we feel in our brief legislative history, the impact of Norris-LaGuardia. We have argued extensively the matters leading up to Norris-LaGuardia, and have analyzed the classic work on the subject of labor injunction by Frank Fuerger and Green. I'm sorry to backtrack a little bit. Before you get into Norris-LaGuardia, I'm going a little further with just Douglas' inquiry. A little different aspect of it. With respect to the individual employees, who, as you say, for several reasons cannot be made defendants here, could an individual employee covered by a collective bargaining agreement which contained a no lockout fraud, sue as an individual, sue the employer under Section 301 if he were locked out? I would say this, Your Honor, that the commitment regarding the lockout runs to the union. And this is my own view of the matter, that the proper party would be the union to sue. Now, the individual's claim, I would suggest, would have to operate through the grievance procedure. I assume there was no grievance. This is my view of the subject. What? This is my view of the subject. What grievance procedure? I'm assuming there is no grievance procedure. There is no grievance procedure, but there's no lockout. There's no lockout. I think it is the responsibility of the union to bring that suit. You think an individual employee could not bring a suit? No. I would say this, that if the union did not bring the suit and there was a fair basis that the suit should be brought, that the individual may be able to prevail upon the courts to force the employer's hand, the union's hand, rather. Kind of a derivative suit. Yes, of some time. Now, you do have this situation occurring, Your Honor, in the Westinghouse, that there is this area where the courts say, well, individuals have certain vested, very personal rights, like a claim for back wages. They've been fired, and the union shouldn't be forced to bring this type of action. It's a very personalized matter. If the individual was bringing the suit in order to question the validity of the lockout under the collective bargaining contract, I would say that the appropriate party is the union, because the issue basically is a collective bargaining one. If there was no question that the lockout was illegal, and this individual said, well, it's been proven the lockout's been illegal, well, I haven't gotten my wages, this might be considered a very personalized dispute, no longer a collective bargaining issue. I think what we have to look at here is the issue raised, an issue under the collective bargaining contract. Well, but the union hasn't been locked out. The employees have been locked out. Yes, but the commitment... And this fellow says, I've been locked out, and I'm not suing for wages. I'm suing for the right to get in there and work for not only wages, but for all the other things that come to me under the collective bargaining agreement. We submit, Mr. Justice Stewart, that the no lockout pledge runs to the contracting party, and the contracting party in this case is the organization. Now, if we presume that the employer, as was said in the Drake Bakery case, signs an affidavit that I've breached the no lockout clause, and there's no collective bargaining dispute, and the individual says I should get money for it, then possibly we've taken it out of the area of collective bargaining disputes. But I think otherwise, if there was a question, has the employer actually locked out the employees or breached the contract or to extend the no lockout pledge, the appropriate party is the union. This is my belief. Otherwise, I think we will have state courts deciding major collective bargaining issues by virtue of one individual filing an individual lawsuit that is collective bargaining contract. Well, could an employee bring this suit in the federal courts under Section 301? I can't see how, Your Honor, because Section 301 provides for only suits between employers and labor organizations. No, it doesn't. No, you look at the way it's written. Suits for violation of? Of collective bargaining contracts between employers and labor organizations. It doesn't say who shall bring them, who shall be the plaintiff or who shall be the defendant. Well, I would say this, Your Honor, that in this, the way I would interpret the import of Section 301 is that if an individual brought a suit for breach of the collective bargaining contract, unless the individual has made a party to the collective bargaining contract, he doesn't have stature to be a party to that lawsuit. Would this matter standing be something which the federal district court should refer to state law to determine the answer to? I would... I'm not sure I understand your question, Your Honor. You say... I think you said he didn't have stature, and I suppose you said he didn't have standing? That's right. Is this a question of federal law? As to whether or not he is a party to... He has standing to sue. Well, I think the federal courts could make a determination whether the individual is a party to the collective bargaining contract, and if the federal courts were to make such a determination, then the individual would have standing. I would suggest that... The statute... Under section... I think I'm right in saying that the statute doesn't, certainly by its terms, specify who the plaintiff needs to be. I think it says suits for violation of contracts made by labor organizations. I was wondering if an individual employee could bring such a suit in a federal court under section 301. Yes. If he had been locked out by an employer who had signed a collective bargaining agreement saying he would not lock out his employees. And my answer would have to remain, Your Honor, that if an individual brought a suit for breach of the collective bargaining contract, the first question would have to be asked, are you a party to the collective bargaining contract? And I would say that an individual, unless he is representing the party to the collective bargaining contract, is not a party. he might be what we might call a third-party beneficiary of some kind. Yes, he might. And he's the one who's been hurt, isn't he? Yes, but I would say this, that he is not bringing a suit for breach of the collective bargaining contract. If that determination has been made, and he says, by virtue of this breach of the suit of the collective bargaining contract, I have been deprived of certain wages, then I think we no longer have a collective bargaining dispute. Well, I think we're, I've led you a little field, but I was just testing out the first part of your argument that no suit could ever be brought against individuals. I wondered if individuals as plaintiffs could bring them according to you. I would say this, Your Honor, that I think it would be very, very unfortunate if the courts were to interpret Section 301 as to allow individual union members to flood the federal courts with suits or breaches of collective bargaining contracts. There's 1,700 employees at this one refinery. I would like to make some general comments on the injunction issue. As I was saying, I don't, do not, I think that the Norris, LaGuardia, and Clayton Act clearly applies to the requested injunction relief in count three. But in this part of the oral presentation, we believe it is important to stress the considerations involved in deciding whether federal courts should be allowed to embark upon this species of injunction. I wish to remind the court that there was no work stoppage at any time during the course of this lawsuit, unlike Yellow Transit. this injunction is only towards future activities which have not occurred and may never occur. Now, the employer argues regarding Norris, LaGuardia, that Norris, LaGuardia was never intended to cover unlawful labor disputes. That's not a question of whether Section 301 has impliedly repealed Norris, LaGuardia, but that Norris, LaGuardia never meant to cover this area. And that Norris, LaGuardia, was concerned only with so-called lawful disputes. Now, we concede, and there's been a number of cases on this point, that Norris, LaGuardia, wasn't meant to interfere with injunctions where violence has occurred or criminal violations have occurred. But this area of legality is another question. Now, we submit that the employer misconceives the purposes of Norris, LaGuardia. The Clayton Act was passed in 1914. The Clayton Act, as applied to labor organizations or labor disputes, stated that injunctions couldn't be issued in disputes between employers and employees. Now, it's a matter of history that, by and large, the Clayton Act was interpreted by the courts as to be applied only to legal labor activities. And by and large, the courts, before 1932, had interpreted the Clayton Act in such a way that it said, injunctions are only prohibited in those activities, labor activities, that were lawful before Clayton Act. Now, the Norris-LaGuardia Act was passed basically to cure this defect in the Clayton Act as had been interpreted by the courts. The classic work on the subject, the labor injunction by Frankfurter and Green, the entire thesis of the book, is that the need for the Norris-LaGuardia Act is because the courts had been deciding that the Clayton Act applied only to legal disputes. And the entire thesis of the book was that there was a need to stop injunctions from occurring by the courts in situations where the courts would issue peremptory restraining orders solely on employer affidavits without hearing. And then, several months later, there would be an argument of the merits, but by now the labor dispute had already been broken and whether or not the unions had a valid claim had already been vitiated. I wish to give an example of the effective Norris-LaGuardia Act. Let's take secondary boycotts. Before Clayton Act and after Clayton Act, the courts by and large held that for unions to participate in any form of secondary boycott was illegal. Now, Norris-LaGuardia did not make secondary boycotts legal, but after Norris-LaGuardia, the courts could no longer issue injunctions to restrain secondary boycotts. This would allow, presumably, employers to sue the unions or individuals for participating in breaches of secondary boycotts where there was no labor contract. It wasn't until 1935 with the passage of the Wagner Act that secondary boycotts, or at least a variety of them, so-called, were legalized. And here you had a joining of anti-injunction provisions and the legalization of secondary boycotts. Now, in 1947, Congress held that secondary boycotts, at least a good number of them, were unlawful. But Congress did not then simply say, well, from now on, Norris-LaGuardia doesn't apply, and from now on you can sue. By then, there had been established the National Labor Relations Board. Congress allowed for restraining orders, but had to be done through the procedures of the National Labor Relations Board, and the National Labor Relations Board has to be the initiating party. so that the argument that Norris-LaGuardia applies only to so-called legal disputes is clearly incorrect in terms of the history before and after Norris-LaGuardia and the reasons for passing it. Now, even if we are satisfied that a wildcat, that is, as Mr. Meyer and the Drake Bakery's argument adequately showed, not a strike for economic purposes, any kind of work stoppage that takes place during the course of a collective bargaining contract, developing out of the spontaneous friction and interaction of employees and supervisors, even if we say it is socially undesirable, I do not submit that the answer lies in allowing the courts to issue wholesale injunctions or allowing the courts to exercise injunctions, preliminary restraining orders, preemptory restraining orders on the basis of affidavits. What, even if we said, and as a matter of social policy, that some type of restraint should be put on these type of work stoppages, what are the possibilities? Are restraining orders and contempt citations to run against individual union officials as well as members of the organization and the organizations themselves? The type of injunction requested here would run against organizations, would run against union officials, would also run against members and any new employees that come in the plan. Do we really mean that granting the injunction request here would allow contempt citations to issue preemptory against all these people? But, what if we say, the such an injunction should issue? Does this mean that a work stoppage occurs three, four, five years from now? The employer comes running into court with a contempt citation for this injunction the employer has requested. The people are out on the street. This means that they refuse to return to work they are then in contempt of court. This would be solely clearly, so clearly violent of the 13th Amendment, I don't think we have to discuss it. It would be specific performance of personal service commitments. But what does it mean to say you're having an injunction running against individuals? Then we ask ourselves, well, we won't issue injunctions against individuals, only be against the organizations. What does it mean to say that the organizations are enjoined from encouraging strikes? These are wildcats, remember. In yellow transit, there was no question that the company called the work salvages to dispute whether they had the right to. Here's a wildcat situation. It happened and it stopped. By its very nature, the union maintains we didn't call it. This is the nature of wildcats.
